items.title: 30.4.2 High-Resolution 1H NMR and Splitting of Peaks

source_refs.note: Topic 30.4.2 with Table 30.2 and Quick Check 30.3, answered (PDF 207-209); Figures 30.5 and 30.6 and the table's peak shapes are redrawn. Answers need review.

blocks.text: NMR signals are affected not only by nearby electrons but also by protons on the adjacent atoms. In a high-resolution spectrum each peak is often a cluster of sub-peaks, because the signal is split by the protons (1H) on adjacent carbon atoms. The splitting into multiple peaks (doublets, triplets, quartets) shows the number of protons on the neighbouring carbon atom. The number of sub-peaks follows the n + 1 rule: a signal usually splits into n + 1 sub-peaks, where n is the number of protons on the adjacent carbon atoms.

In the high-resolution spectrum of ethanol the -CH3 peak is split into three sub-peaks (a triplet), because the adjacent carbon has 2 protons (2 + 1 = 3), and the -CH2- peak into four sub-peaks (a quartet), because its adjacent carbon has 3 protons (3 + 1 = 4). The -OH signal is not split, because its hydrogen is bonded to oxygen rather than carbon.

blocks.alt: High-resolution spectrum on a scale from 9 to 0 with the formula CH3 - CH2 - OH. A tall single peak labelled 1H at about 5.4, a group of four sub-peaks labelled 2H at about 3.6, and a group of three sub-peaks labelled 3H at about 1.2.
blocks.caption: Figure 30.5: High-resolution 1H NMR spectrum of ethanol (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 30.5).

blocks.text: -OH and -NH protons usually do not show splitting and appear as singlets. Chemically equivalent protons do not split each other either: ethane, CH3-CH3, gives a single unsplit peak, because all its hydrogens are equivalent.

blocks.alt: A spectrum on a scale from 3 to 0 with the formula H3C-CH3 and one sharp, unsplit peak near 0.9.
blocks.caption: Figure 30.6: High-resolution 1H NMR spectrum of ethane (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 30.6).

blocks.alt: The appearance of split peaks from Table 30.2: one peak (singlet, s, n = 0), two equal peaks (doublet, d, n = 1), three peaks with the middle one tallest (triplet, t, n = 2), and four peaks with the inner two tallest (quartet, q, n = 3).
blocks.caption: Table 30.2, Appearance of Split Peak (original drawing after the peak shapes printed in Table 30.2).

items: A signal in a 1H NMR spectrum is a quartet. How many adjacent, equivalent protons are there?
